questions.question: List four properties of acids and give three examples of weak acids found in food and two strong acids.
questions.expected_answer: Acids taste sour (never test by tasting); turn blue litmus red; react with some metals to give hydrogen gas; react with carbonates such as baking soda to give carbon dioxide; strong acids are corrosive; conduct electricity in solution. Weak acids: citric acid (lemons), acetic acid (vinegar), lactic acid (amasi, yoghurt), carbonic acid (cooldrinks), ascorbic acid (vitamin C). Strong acids: hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid (car batteries), nitric acid.

questions.question: Describe the properties of bases, define an alkali and give three household bases with their uses.
questions.expected_answer: Bases taste bitter and feel slippery or soapy (never test by tasting or touching); turn red litmus blue; neutralise acids; strong bases are corrosive. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water. Examples: baking soda (baking, mild cleaning, indigestion); antacids or milk of magnesia (neutralise stomach acid); soap and detergents (remove grease); toothpaste; household ammonia (glass cleaner); caustic soda (drain and oven cleaner, strong and dangerous).

questions.question: Define neutral and neutralisation, state the products of neutralisation, and describe two everyday uses.
questions.expected_answer: A neutral substance is neither acidic nor basic and does not change the colour of red or blue litmus (pure water, sugar solution). Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base in which their properties cancel; the products are a salt and water (hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide gives sodium chloride + water). Uses: antacids neutralise excess stomach acid; toothpaste neutralises acids from mouth bacteria; farmers add lime to neutralise acidic soil; factories and mines neutralise acidic waste with lime.
